newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Alaska officials want people to visit -- in winter.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Alaska officials want people to visit -- in winter.

text.p: Looking for a place to escape the winter doldrums? How about Alaska, the place where many think winter and its doldrums were invented?

The suggestion is serious; tourism promoters want people to think of cheery outdoors adventures, not frigid Arctic darkness or cabin fever. "This is the Alaska that they've heard about. It's snowing, it's cold, there's dog sleds," said Tom Garrett, director of the Alaska Division of Tourism.
The division is sincere enough that it is starting a special Alaska promotion in sunny Phoenix. "The theme is, 'The world's biggest white sale,'" Garrett said optimistically.

Tourism operators suggest visitors might want to partake in the same winter recreation that occupies residents during the snowy months -- skiing, dog-sledding, snowshoeing and viewing wildlife in scenic wildlands.

"We're really trying to educate people that it's not as cold and dark as they think it is," said Allison Knox, public-relations manager for Alyeska Resort, located in a narrow glacier-carved valley about 40 miles (65 km) south of Anchorage. She and other Anchorage-area tourism boosters assure sceptics that this part of the state, at about the same latitude as Oslo, benefits from the moderating influences of warm Pacific currents.
COLD IS A HARD SELL
It may be a tough sell this winter, which so far has been the coldest since 1982. But temperature questions aside, promoting winter is logical for the Alaska tourism industry.

Three-quarters of the approximately 1 million people who visit Alaska come between May and September, crowding major tourist stops, hotels and lodges, state figures show. Many of those sites stand nearly empty in winter. And, while summer tourism is booming, with annual growth of about 7.5 percent, winter tourism growth is only a quarter of that.

Still, some niche markets have emerged for the mostly young and sporty Alaska winter tourists. The steep Chugach mountains that tower over Girdwood and nurtured Olympic downhill champion Tommy Moe draw expert skiers who want to avoid ordinary resorts.

Anchorage's Fur Rendezvous, a carnival held each February, and the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race, held in March, attract dog-sledding fans from around the world. Farther north, Fairbanks gets thousands of Japanese tourists every winter to view the Aurora Borealis in the clear night skies. Last winter, 3,000 to 4,000 Japanese visitors came to Mount Aurora/Skiland, a tiny family ski area on the city's outskirts, to watch the celestial phenomenon.

"They pay to stand in the dark and watch," said Skiland owner Brenda Birdsall. "Even when temperatures dip to well below freezing, they just put on more layers of clothing and go outside. They're great people to have as your guests because they're just so polite and kind."

Aurora watchers at the ski area have included a movie star, film crews and Japan's only astronaut, Steve Birdsall, Brenda's husband, said. "He saw the Aurora from the top side and he wanted to see it from the bottom," Birdsall said.
At Girdwood's Alyeska Resort, guests at the new luxury hotel can get wake-up calls for Aurora displays. But even here at Alaska's biggest ski resort, summer business dominates.

"Summer looks very good. Winter, we need to be more aggressive," conceded Chris Von Imhof, the resort's general manager. Alyeska, owned by Japan's Seibu Group, has invested a reported $70 million in a luxurious Prince Hotel, elegant restaurants, a tram and on-mountain improvements, but its winter market is overwhelmingly from in-state.
MORE DEVELOPMENT SEEN

Alyeska could draw more winter adventurers with helicopter ski tours on nearby slopes, an activity that may start this spring if the U.S. Forest Service grants permits. Eventually, Alyeska might install a sister ski resort up the valley, Von Imhof said.
Success depends in part on getting direct passenger flights from ski-mad Japan, source of many winter visitors to Whistler and other British Columbia ski resorts, he said.

Gov. Tony Knowles has proposed a $1 million reward to the first carrier to establish such a year-round passenger link. Knowles is also asking the U.S. government to drop its visa requirement for South Koreans as another inducement for year-round Alaska tourism.

Von Imhof said late winter and spring are the most attractive for visitors. He writes off the coldest and darkest months as fated to be quiet in Alaska, except for the few curious visitors like the Aurora watchers and the usual hardy Alaskans seeking cabin-fever diversions.
"For the rest of the world, I think, we should concentrate on February, March and April," he said.
